title: Building the Index
description: Build search indexes at scale with MapReduce, inverted index structure with posting lists, skip pointers, index compression techniques, and distributed index sharding strategies.

segments.text: The inverted index is the heart of every search engine. Instead of mapping documents to words — which is useless for search — it maps words to documents. The term 'distributed' maps to a posting list: document 42 at position 7, document 108 at position 3, document 9001 at position 15. Google's index covers hundreds of billions of web pages.

Each posting list entry stores: document ID, term frequency in that document, and positions where the term appears. Positions enable phrase queries — 'distributed systems' requires both words appearing adjacent. The posting list is sorted by document ID for efficient intersection. Querying 'distributed AND systems' intersects two sorted lists.

Building the index at web scale uses MapReduce. Map phase: each mapper processes a batch of documents, emits (term, document_ID, positions) tuples. Reduce phase: each reducer collects all postings for a term and builds the sorted posting list. Google's original MapReduce paper described exactly this use case. Modern systems use Spark for faster iteration.

Posting list intersection is the hot path. For a query with two terms, you're intersecting two sorted lists. Skip pointers speed this up — every sqrt(N) entries, insert a pointer to skip ahead. When searching for the intersection point, instead of scanning linearly, you skip forward. This reduces intersection time from O(N) to O(sqrt(N)).

Index compression is critical — an uncompressed index for the web would be petabytes. Variable-length integer encoding stores small numbers in one byte and large numbers in more bytes. PForDelta compresses blocks of one hundred twenty-eight document IDs by storing the delta between consecutive IDs — since sorted IDs have small gaps. Compression ratios of three to five times are typical.

Your index has ten billion documents and one hundred million unique terms. The full index is fifty terabytes. A single machine can hold two terabytes in memory. How would you distribute this index across machines?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you shard a 50TB search index across machines? By document or by term?

segments.text: Two sharding strategies. Document-partitioned: each shard holds all terms for a subset of documents. A query goes to every shard, each returns top-K results, and a coordinator merges. Term-partitioned: each shard holds posting lists for a subset of terms. A query touches only the relevant shards. Google uses document-partitioned because it's simpler and more balanced.

Each shard is replicated for both durability and read throughput. With three replicas per shard and twenty-five shards, that's seventy-five index servers. Queries are load-balanced across replicas. If a replica fails, the other two handle the load. Rebalancing only reshuffles data for that shard, not the entire index.

Rebuilding the entire index for every new document is impractical. Use a tiered index: a small in-memory index for real-time updates and a large on-disk index for the bulk. Periodically merge the in-memory index into the on-disk index. Elasticsearch does this with Lucene segments — new documents go to small segments that are periodically merged into larger ones.

Design the indexing pipeline for an e-commerce search engine with fifty million products, updates every five minutes, and sub-fifty-millisecond query latency requirements. What's your index structure and update strategy?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a search index for 50M products with 5-minute update freshness and sub-50ms queries.

segments.text: Search indexing at scale is inverted indexes with posting lists, built via MapReduce or Spark, compressed with varint and PForDelta, accelerated with skip pointers, sharded by document across machines, and kept fresh with incremental tiered merging.
